Host defense against viral pathogens is an essential function for all living organisms. In cell-intrinsic innate immunity, dedicated sensor proteins recognize molecular signatures of infection and communicate to downstream adaptor or effector proteins to activate immune defense. Remarkably, recent evidence demonstrates that much of the core machinery of innate immunity is shared across eukaryotic and prokaryotic domains of life. Here, we review a pioneering example of evolutionary conservation in innate immunity: the animal cGAS-STING (cyclic GMP-AMP synthase–stimulator of interferon genes) signaling pathway and its ancestor in bacteria, CBASS (cyclic nucleotide-based antiphage signaling system) antiphage defense. We discuss the unique mechanism by which animal cGLRs (cGAS-like receptors) and bacterial CD-NTases (cGAS/dinucleotide-cyclase in Vibrio (DncV)-like nucleotidyltransferases) in these pathways link pathogen detection with immune activation using nucleotide second messenger signals. Comparing the biochemical, structural, and mechanistic details of cGAS-STING, cGLR signaling, and CBASS, we highlight emerging questions in the field and

cGAS-STING (cyclic GMP-AMP synthase–stimulator of interferon genes) is an immune pathway in animal cells that controls the cellular response to cytosolic double-stranded (ds) DNA (1–3). Upon directly binding to dsDNA, the enzyme cGAS (cyclic GMP-AMP synthase) is activated to synthesize the nucleotide second messenger 2′3′-cGAMP (cG[2′–5′]pA[3′–5′]p) (4–7). 2′3′-cGAMP is recognized by the adaptor protein STING (stimulator of interferon genes), which then recruits the kinase TBK1 (TANK-binding kinase 1) and the transcription factors IRF3 (interferon regulatory factor 3) and NF-κB (nuclear factor κ-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells) to activate type I IFN (interferon) and an antiviral signaling program (8). Most animal species encode multiple homologs of cGAS, known as cGLRs (cGAS-like receptors) (9, 10). The best characterized of these, Drosophila melanogaster cGLR1, functions as a dsRNA sensor and synthesizes a distinct nucleotide signal, 3′2′-cGAMP, to activate STING and antiviral immunity (9, 10). Divergent cGLRs encoded throughout the animal kingdom recognize dsDNA, dsRNA, or as-yet-unidentified ligands and synthesize a variety of nucleotide second messengers that bind STING proteins encoded within corresponding species (11). Thus, cGLR-STING signaling is a broadly conserved mechanism in metazoan innate immunity that enables animals to detect diverse molecular cues of pathogen infection and use nucleotide signals to control the immune response (Figure 1).

Identification of ancient cGAS and STING proteins in bacteria led to the striking discovery that many metazoan innate immune pathways first evolved in prokaryotes as antibacteriophage (antiphage) defense systems (12–14). Bacterial cGAS homologs, known as CD-NTases (cGAS/DncV-like nucleotidyltransferases), control a form of antiphage defense named CBASS (cyclic oligonucleotide-based antiphage signaling system) that is present in an estimated ∼14.4% of sequenced bacterial and archaeal species (12, 15, 16). Similar to cGAS recognition of viral infection in animal cells, bacterial CD-NTases sense phage infection and synthesize a diversity of nucleotide signals to activate Cap (CD-NTase-associated protein) effectors (13, 17, 18). CBASS systems encode diverse Cap effectors that upon activation degrade essential cellular components to induce abortive infection, thereby inhibiting the production of progeny phage particles within the infected cell and limiting viral spread (13, 17–19) (Figure 1). CBASS systems often include ancillary Cap proteins that regulate CD-NTase activation, and systems can be stratified into four types based on conserved operon structure (for an explanation, see the caption to Figure 1) (15).

In many classical forms of innate immunity, protein sensors detect molecules associated with infection and then transmit immune activation through direct protein–protein interactions (Figure 1). Hallmark examples include mammalian Toll-like receptors that directly bind adaptor proteins to control downstream signal transduction and the transcription of antiviral genes (20, 21).Similarly,many bacterial defense systems function through direct protein–protein interactions to form complexes that both sense and degrade target phage molecules (19,22,23).cGLR-STING and CBASS immunity are two systems that subvert this paradigm: Instead of protein–protein interactions, immune activation is communicated via the production and reception of a diffusible nucleotide second messenger. Additional forms of immunity using nucleotide second messengers, including Type III CRISPR (24, 25), Pycsar (26), and Thoeris (27, 28) antiphage defense systems in bacteria and OAS (oligoadenylate synthase) enzymes (29) in animal cells, highlight the central evolutionary role of second messenger signals in immune defense.

Nucleotide second messenger signaling in cGLR-STING and CBASS immunity. In animals, cGAS and cGLR pattern recognition receptors detect molecular signatures of infection and synthesize cyclic dinucleotide second messengers. Upon binding nucleotide second messenger signals, the adaptor protein STING activates antiviral transcription programs through NF-κB and IRF3. cGLR enzymes and STING are encoded at separate genomic loci: In humans cGAS is encoded on C6, and STING is encoded on C5. In bacterial CBASS systems, CD-NTase enzymes are activated by phage infection to synthesize cyclic di- or trinucleotide second messengers that are specifically recognized by adjacently encoded Cap effectors. Cap effectors target essential cellular components to induce abortive infection and protect bacterial populations from phage infection. CBASS operons universally encode a CD-NTase and an effector protein and are classified by regulatory Cap proteins. Type I systems contain no additional proteins. Type II systems encode Cap2, a protein with homology to eukaryotic ubiquitin-activating E1 proteins and ubiquitin-conjugating E2 proteins, and Cap3, a protein with homology to eukaryotic JAB deubiquitinating isopeptidases. Type III systems encode Cap6, homologous to eukaryotic Trip13 AAA+, and Cap7, homologous to eukaryotic HORMA domains. Some Type III systems additionally encode Cap8, a second divergent HORMA-like protein. Type IV systems encode proteins with predicted roles in converting and exchanging modified nucleobases: Cap9, a protein with a QueC enzymatic domain, and Cap10, a protein with a TGT enzymatic domain. Some Type IV systems additionally encode Cap11, a predicted N-glycosylase/DNA lyase. Cell-intrinsic immune pathways must connect pathogen sensing with a downstream immune response. Many classical pathways rely on direct protein–protein interactions between sensor proteins and adaptor proteins that activate transcription factors to induce antiviral gene programs (eukaryotes) or effector proteins that directly target invading viruses (prokaryotes). Animal cGLR-STING and bacterial CBASS pathways subvert this paradigm: Sensor cGLRs or CD-NTases communicate immune activation to downstream adaptor or effector proteins using nucleotide second messenger signals. 2. PATHOGEN SENSING AND REGULATION OF cGLR AND CD-NTase ACTIVITY
2.1. Detection of Infection by cGLRs and CD-NTases

Animal cGLRs and bacterial CD-NTases function as molecular sensors of pathogen infection.Animal cGLRs directly detect DNA and RNA as pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) (Figure 2). In animal cells, DNA and RNA are important PAMPs, as compartmentalization and modification of nucleic acid are used to regulate cellular function and define self from nonself. Cytosolic dsDNA is a potent danger signal to metazoan cells and can result from self (micronuclei formation and rupture, loss of mitochondrial integrity, cellular stress events) and nonself (viral or bacterial genomic material) sources (8, 30). Human and vertebrate cGAS proteins function as direct sensors of cytosolic dsDNA to play important roles in antitumor immunity and the response to a broad spectrum of viral and bacterial pathogens (2, 31, 32). The discovery of cGLRs as a diverse family of pattern recognition receptors in animals revealed that divergent proteins in this family also function as dsRNA sensors (9, 10). dsRNA is a common PAMP recognized by

The prominent role of DNA sensing in cGAS-dependent animal immunity has led to speculation that bacterial CD-NTases may respond to viral genomic DNA. Although bacteria lack nuclei and genomic compartmentalization, unique base modifications in viral nucleic acids or replication intermediates associated with viral genome replication may provide an opportunity for accurate sensing of foreign DNA (33). However, while activation of a CD-NTase enzyme from Escherichia coli has been reported to be enhanced by DNA (18), there is currently no direct evidence in support of phage genome sensing by CD-NTases. Other nucleic acid species produced during viral replication may serve as molecular cues of infection. It was recently reported that second messenger synthesis by a Staphylococcus schleiferi CD-NTase from Clade E is directly activated by a unique, highly structured viral RNA produced during staphylococcal phage infection, termed the cabRNA (CBASS-activating bacteriophage RNA) (34). This discovery highlights a conserved role for nucleic acid immunity in eukaryotic and prokaryotic domains of life, and nucleic acid sensing by CD-NTases remains an important area of investigation. Interestingly, selection for phages resistant to CBASS immunity and related bacterial immune systems demonstrated that mutations in viral capsid proteins enable evasion of antiphage defense, suggesting that detection of phage capsids may trigger CBASS activation (26, 34, 35). Direct sensing of phage structural proteins in bacterial Avs-mediated immunity and by CapRel toxinantitoxin operons suggests that conserved viral structures can be broadly recognized as PAMPs by bacterial defense systems (36, 37). However, staphylococcal capsid mutant phages that resist CBASS immunity still produce the CD-NTase-activating RNA, suggesting that capsid mutations mediate immune escape downstream of second messenger production (34). Finally, an important distinction between cGLRs and CD-NTases is that many bacterial CD-NTases are constitutively active in vitro when purified in isolation and in the absence of bound ligands (12). Consistent with this basal in vitro activity, it has been proposed that some CBASS systems function through a guard mechanism in which the depletion of a specific host factor during infection relieves enzymatic inhibition and stimulates nucleotide second messenger synthesis (14, 38). 2.2. Structural Features of cGLRs and CD-NTases

Animal cGLRs and bacterial CD-NTases share a conserved protein architecture in which an N-terminal nucleotidyltransferase core and C-terminal α-helix bundle are bridged by a spine helix to enclose a caged catalytic pocket that supports nucleotide second messenger synthesis (39) (Figure 2). A conserved catalytic triad ([DE]h [DE]h [X50–90] h[DE]h, where h is a hydrophobic amino acid) within this pocket controls nucleotidyltransferase activity. cGLR and CD-NTase enzymes are members of the DNA-polβ superfamily that includes ancestral proteins involved in DNA replication and RNA repair, demonstrating how the fundamental biochemical function of nucleotidyltransferase activity has been co-opted for an immune signaling role.

cGAS and cGLRs directly bind PAMPs through a conserved ligand binding groove along the spine helix (4, 9, 40–44). Bacterial CD-NTases contain a similar putative ligand binding groove, but it is unclear if this feature is responsible for recognition of a phage-associated cue (12, 45, 46). In cGAS and dsRNA-sensing cGLRs, including Drosophila cGLR1, positively charged residues along this groove are responsible for electrostatic interactions with nucleic acids.The cGAS ligand binding groove is further defined by a zinc coordinating motif insertion (Zn-ribbon), which is required for recognition of dsDNA ligands (4,40,41,43,44).The Zn-ribbon insertion is exclusive to vertebrate cGAS enzymes,explaining the ability of these proteins to function as dsDNA sensors. Intriguingly, invertebrate cGLRs from the species Crassostrea gigas and Crassostrea virginica that are closely related to vertebrate cGAS also function as dsDNA sensors. These proteins lack a Znribbon and therefore may sense DNA through a distinct mechanism (11). Diversification of the ligand binding groove throughout metazoan cGLRs likely explains how divergent enzymes detect different molecular patterns (11).

The mechanism of mammalian cGAS activation is well characterized including defined interaction sites controlling recognition of dsDNA, formation of a minimally active 2:2 cGAS–DNA complex, and oligomerization into higher-order states critical for robust 2′3′-cGAMP synthesis (4, 40–44, 47–49). cGAS–DNA interactions are further controlled by an unstructured N-terminal domain that contributes to the formation of liquid condensates to promote cGAS enzymatic activity (48, 50). The molecular mechanism of ligand recognition and activation for other metazoan cGLRs and bacterial CD-NTases is currently uncharacterized. While the global architecture of this protein family is highly conserved, key structural differences between divergent cGLRs and CD-NTases likely control unique aspects of ligand recognition and enzymatic activation.

Unstructured N-terminal extensions are common among vertebrate cGAS proteins,and a subset of other metazoan cGLRs also contain disordered N or C termini. While most cGLRs are encoded as individual enzymatic domains, a select number of cGLRs are appended to second cGLR proteins, or other domains frequently associated with immunity including tetratricopeptide- and ankyrin-repeat modules (11). Ancillary domain fusions and disordered extensions are rare in prokaryotic CD-NTases. A notable exception are the ∼30% of CD-NTases in Type I CBASS operons found fused to a domain of undefined function named AGS-C, which is predicted to have homology to Ig-fold proteins (15, 51, 52). While such N- and C-terminally appended domains in cGLRs and CD-NTases have no defined function, it is possible they contribute to the molecular detection of viral infection and the regulation of nucleotide second messenger synthesis.

Growing evidence suggests that bacterial CD-NTase activation is regulated by auxiliary Cap proteins encoded within CBASS antiphage defense operons (Figure 2). Recently, multiple groups reported that Type II CBASS operons prime CD-NTase enzymatic activity using a reaction that shares remarkable similarity with animal ubiquitin transfer reactions (76–78). During CBASS antiphage defense, Cap2, an accessory protein with structural homology to eukaryotic E1 ubiquitin-activating and E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes,covalently links the CD-NTase C terminus to an unknown substrate in a reaction that promotes a greater than 50-fold upregulation in nucleotide second messenger synthesis in response to phage infection. The Type II CBASS protein Cap3, an accessory protein with structural homology to eukaryotic JAB isopeptidase domains found in deubiquitinating enzymes, cleaves this linkage and downregulates CD-NTase enzymatic activity (76–78). Likewise, Cap6 and Cap7 proteins in Type III CBASS operons exhibit structural homology with eukaryotic TRIP13 (thyroid hormone receptor interactor 13) and HORMA (HOp1p, Rev7p, and MAd2) proteins and control a peptide recognition event that regulates CDNTase activation during antiphage defense (18). Finally, operon transcription and CD-NTase expression can be regulated by WYL domain-containing transcription factors that tune overall gene expression (79). It remains an open question whether phages have evolved mechanisms to specifically target CBASS signaling at the step of CD-NTase activation.
3. NUCLEOTIDE SECOND MESSENGERS IN cGLR AND CBASS IMMUNITY
3.1. Mechanism of Nucleotide Second Messenger Synthesis

A defining feature of cGLR-STING and CBASS is the utilization of a nucleotide second messenger to link pathogen detection with downstream antiviral immunity.Following PAMP recognition, animal cGLRs and bacterial CD-NTases use a single catalytic site to catalyze a conserved multistep reaction resulting in the production of a cyclic dinucleotide or cyclic trinucleotide nucleotide signal (4, 9, 12, 41, 44, 45) (Figure 3). Enzymatic activity is controlled by a conserved triad of aspartate and glutamate residues that coordinate either magnesium or manganese catalytic ions. In each reaction, the 5′ α-phosphate of a nucleotide donor is linked to the 2′ or 3′ hydroxyl of a nucleotide acceptor (forming a 2′–5′ or 3′–5′ phosphodiester bond, respectively). For cyclic dinucleotide signals such as 2′3′-cGAMP and 3′3′-cGAMP, the resulting linear intermediate reorients within the catalytic pocket with donor and acceptor positions reversed for formation of the second bond and cyclization of the final product (4, 12, 45). Nucleotide second messenger synthesis provides distinct advantages within cGLR-STING and CBASS antiviral signaling pathways. First, ribonucleotide substrates are ubiquitous throughout the cell, and thus cGLRs and CD-NTases can rapidly synthesize large quantities of second messenger molecules. Second, cGLR and CD-NTase activation dramatically amplifies initial signaling. For example, activation of a few enzymes of cGAS bound to DNA causes multi-turnover production with more than 750 molecules of 2′3′-cGAMP signal synthesized for each active enzyme (4). Likewise, in response to phage infection, CD-NTases synthesize micromolar levels of nucleotide second messenger signals to rapidly activate cell death effector Cap proteins (13, 17).

While 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds are the common linkage in cellular RNA and DNA, 2′–5′ phosphodiester bonds are rare in biology. 3′–5′ and 2′–5′ phosphodiester linkage specificity is critical to the ability of cGLR and CDNTase nucleotide second messengers to interact with receptors with high affinity and control downstream immune signaling (7,17,86).2′–5′ phosphodiester linkages also play a key role in differentiating nucleotide immune signaling pathways and preventing cross talk with other endogenous host cell processes. Notably, a role for 2′–5′ linkages in immune signaling was first identified in the linear 2′–5′ oligoadenylate product synthesized by mammalian OAS1 (oligoadenylate synthase 1) (164,165).OAS1 is a double-stranded RNA sensor that signals through the downstream receptor RNase L to block viral replication (29). Although initial structures of human cGAS revealed structural similarity with OAS1, cGAS and animal cGLRs share significantly greater structural homology with bacterial CDNTases, demonstrating a closer evolutionary relationship between bacterial CBASS immunity and animal cGLRSTING signaling than with OAS1 RNA sensing (9).

Additionally, nucleotide second messenger synthesis in animals results in an elevated immune response that spreads as cGLR-produced nucleotide signals are transferred between gap junctions of neighboring cells and imported into immune cells (82–85). No extracellular roles are known for CD-NTase nucleotide signals in bacteria. Finally, nucleotide second messenger synthesis removes the need for direct protein–protein interactions and enables sensor cGLR and CD-NTase proteins to evolve independently from downstream immune adaptor and cell death effector proteins. Most animals encode multiple cGLR proteins (commonly 2–4 cGLRs, more than 40 cGLRs in some select species), and some bacterial CBASS operons encode two unique CD-NTases, suggesting pathogen sensing can be enhanced by sensor protein duplication (11, 12). In animal cGLR-STING immunity, duplication of adaptor genes additionally allows cGLR nucleotide second messengers to signal through multiple STING receptors and potentially distinct downstream pathways (11). Likewise, in bacterial CBASS, nucleotide signal production enables Cap proteins to be rapidly exchanged between operons to diversify CBASS systems and expand the repertoire of effectors used to inhibit phage replication (15, 17). Together these unique properties of nucleotide-based immune signaling help explain evolutionary selection of these pathways across divergent kingdoms of life.
3.2. Diversity of Nucleotide Second Messengers in Animals and Bacteria

cGLRs and CD-NTases synthesize a remarkable array of distinct nucleotide second messengers (Figure 3). 2′3′-cGAMP is the major product of vertebrate cGAS enzymes and is thought to be the most common nucleotide second messenger controlling cGLR-STING immunity in animals (5–7, 11, 86, 87). Biochemical screening of hundreds of cGLRs encoded throughout the metazoan kingdom demonstrates that both DNA- and RNA-sensing enzymes from diverse species synthesize 2′3′-cGAMP (11). Although 2′3′-cGAMP was initially assumed to be the exclusive nucleotide second messenger in metazoan pathways, it was recently discovered that Drosophila cGLR1 synthesizes a distinct chemical isomer of cGAMP, 3′2′-cGAMP (cG[3′–5′]pA[2′–5′]p) (9). cGLR1 synthesizes 3′2′-cGAMP using the opposite nucleobase reaction order compared to cGAS, selecting for the reverse donor and acceptor substrates in the synthesis of the first phosphodiester bond.Animal cGLR-produced nucleotide signals are now known to include pyrimidine substrates and distinct combinations of 3′–5′ and 2′–5′ phosphodiester linkages. For example, a cGLR from C.virginica synthesizes 2′3′ cyclic UMP-AMP (2′3′-cUA) in response to the ligand dsDNA while a cGLR from Stylophora pistillata synthesizes 3′3′-cUA in response to the ligand dsRNA (11). Analysis of these cGLR enzymes underscores that a diversity of nucleotide second messenger signals likely remain to be discovered in animal biology.

Bacterial CBASS systems signal through an exceptionally wide array of distinct nucleotide second messengers, with 12 confirmed signals identified and more than 180 possible signals predicted (38). First discovered in Vibrio cholerae, the most common CD-NTase nucleotide signal is the product 3′3′-cGAMP (45, 88). However, bacterial CD-NTase enzymes can utilize all four nucleobases, A, C, G, and U, and can incorporate both 3′–5′ and 2′–5′ linkages (12, 17). CDNTase nucleotide second messengers additionally include cyclic trinucleotide signals, with several CD-NTase enzymes, particularly in Clades C and D, synthesizing cyclic trinucleotides 3′3′3′c-AMP-AMP-GMP (3′3′3′-cAAG) and 3′3′3′-c-AMP-AMP-AMP (3′3′3′-cAAA) (12, 89). Cyclic trinucleotides are also synthesized in Type III CRISPR immune systems,and CBASS and CRISPR operons share evolutionarily related effector proteins that respond to these nucleotide signals (17, 90). The mammalian cyclic nucleotide receptor RECON (reductase controlling NF-κB) can sense bacterial 3′3′3′-cAAG and 3′3′3′-cAAA (12, 91), but endogenous cyclic trinucleotide products have thus far not been identified in metazoan immunity. 3.3. Role of Nucleotide Messengers as Immunotransmitters

A unique aspect of nucleotide second messengers is the ability to control both intracellular and intercellular immune signaling (Figure 3). As charged small molecules, nucleotide second messengers cannot passively permeate cellular membranes. In animals, the cGAS product 2′3′cGAMP can be transferred between gap junctions formed between closely linked cells (82). Additionally, 2′3′-cGAMP is actively exported by the channel ABCC1 (ATP-binding Cassette subfamily C member 1) and is released upon cell death to create an extracellular pool of nucleotide signal (93). Multiple channels including SLC19A1 (Solute Carrier family 19 member 1) and SLC46A2 (Solute Carrier family 46 member 2) family channels as well as LRRC8A:C/E (Leucine-Rich-Repeat containing protein family 8 A:C/E) heterodimers import 2′3′-cGAMP and are particularly important for the role of cGAS and 2′3′-cGAMP signaling in antitumor immunity (83–85, 94). Different 2′3′-cGAMP import channels have varied cell type–specific expression profiles and exhibit distinct biochemical properties that influence the ability of cells to respond to extracellular nucleotide signaling (85). The level of extracellular 2′3′-cGAMP is regulated by the enzyme ENPP1 (ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase phosphodiesterase 1) (95, 96). ENPP1 exists as a dimer tethered to the extracellular membrane or as a secreted protein abundant in plasma and robustly cleaves both 2′–5′ and 3′–5′ bonds of extracellular 2′3′-cGAMP, rendering GMP and AMP molecules that cannot activate STING (96). Notably, 2′3′-cGAMP can also confer longerrange cell-cell immunity as a passenger in viral particles. Upon cGAS activation in virally infected cells, 2′3′-cGAMP is packaged in progeny virions and delivered to the cytoplasm of subsequently infected cells where it directly activates STING to initiate antiviral immunity (97, 98).

To date, intercellular signaling roles have not yet been defined for other cGLR or CBASS nucleotide second messengers in animals or bacteria. However, studies in Drosophila support uptake of extracellular cyclic dinucleotide signals (99), and given that many of the characterized mammalian transport channels are broadly conserved in the metazoan lineage, it is likely that other cGLR products function as immunotransmitters much like 2′3′-cGAMP. Despite living as singlecell organisms, bacteria frequently grow in clonal patches and communicate with other colony members using extracellular chemical communication systems (e.g., quorum sensing). However, given that CBASS nucleotide second messengers control effector-induced cell death, it is unclear that CD-NTase products would function as advantageous intercellular signals.

4. DETECTION OF NUCLEOTIDE IMMUNE SIGNALS BY DOWNSTREAM RECEPTORS
4.1. Functional Domains in Animal and Bacterial Nucleotide Second Messenger Receptors

Nucleotide second messengers synthesized by cGLRs and CD-NTases directly bind and activate receptors to control downstream immunity through signaling cascades or direct effector functions (Figure 4). In metazoans, STING is the major receptor of endogenously synthesized cGLR nucleotide signals. Animal STING proteins form obligate homodimers and contain N-terminal transmembrane (TM) domains that localize the receptor to the ER (endoplasmic reticulum), a central ligand binding domain that binds nucleotide second messengers, and an unstructured Cterminal tail (CTT) that controls the recruitment and activation of downstream signaling kinases (1, 3, 105, 106). Invertebrate STING proteins do not contain a CTT, and thus it is currently unclear how these receptors control immune signaling (87, 107, 108). The STING cyclic dinucleotide binding domain evolved in bacteria as a CBASS receptor, and some bacterial STING proteins are appended to a TIR (Toll-interleukin-1 receptor) domain that cleaves the essential metabolite NAD and causes cell death (14). Intriguingly, several invertebrate STING proteins also contain an N-terminal TIR domain, but the immune mechanism of animal TIR-STING proteins remains an open question (14).

In bacterial CBASS immunity, most Cap protein nucleotide second messenger receptors are composed of discrete sensor domains that directly bind nucleotide second messengers and effector domains that target essential cellular machinery to control antiphage defense (17). 4.2. Molecular Mechanism of Nucleotide Second Messenger Recognition

Diverse protein domains have evolved to specifically recognize the vast diversity of nucleotide second messengers synthesized in cGLR-STING and CBASS immunity (Figure 4). In animal immunity, the major nucleotide second messenger receptor STING forms a homodimeric, Vshaped complex with a deep central pocket for cyclic dinucleotide recognition (7, 9, 11, 14, 86, 87, 111, 112). Upon high-affinity recognition of endogenous cGLR-produced nucleotide signals, the STING β-strand lid closes over the top of the bound ligand and each STING monomer rotates inward to create a compact configuration that seals the nucleotide second messenger binding pocket (7, 9, 86). A network of protein–ligand contacts controls selective recognition of cyclic dinucleotides including stacking interactions between aromatic residues and each nucleobase, and polar contacts at the base of the pocket that read out phosphodiester linkage specificity (7, 9, 11, 14, 86, 87, 111, 112). Substitutions of specific polar residues at the base of the ligand binding pocket explain the specificity of animal STING proteins for distinct endogenous cGLR signals (9, 11), and variations in conserved arginine residues within human STING are known to alter nucleotide second messenger affinity (7,86).Most animals (88%) encode a single STING protein; however, some animal species have an expanded repertoire of cGLR-STING pathways including the coral S. pistillata, which encodes 42 cGLRs and 7 STINGs (11). In addition to detection of endogenous immune signals,animal STING proteins can also more weakly recognize bacterial cyclic dinucleotide ligands including 3′3′-c-di-GMP, 3′3′-c-di-AMP, and the CBASS signal 3′3′-cGAMP (5, 6, 105). RECON additionally recognizes CBASS signals including 3′3′-cUA and the cyclic trinucleotide signals 3′3′3′-cAAA and 3′3′3′-cAAG (12), but thus far the receptor is not known to respond to endogenous cGLR signaling products. RECON functions as a monomer, binding nucleotide second messengers in the same pockets that control adenine and nicotinamide recognition during normal oxidoreductase catalytic function (91). Several RECON homologs exist in human cells, but these proteins have no defined function, suggesting possible yet-undiscovered roles in cGLR signaling and animal innate immunity.

STING proteins are functional receptors in CBASS immunity, demonstrating that STING cyclic dinucleotide recognition originated in bacteria (14). Bacterial and animal STING proteins exhibit striking structural homology and share a conserved mechanism of signal recognition within the homodimeric V-shaped ligand binding pocket. All characterized bacterial STING proteins selectively recognize 3′3′-c-di-GMP, suggesting that the STING homodimer configuration may have originally evolved to bind twofold symmetric nucleotide ligands (14, 109, 118). STING receptors in CBASS are rare, accounting for nucleotide second messenger recognition in less than 5% of CBASS operons (14). The most common CBASS receptors contain a nucleotide second messenger binding domain named SAVED (present in ∼30% of all operons) (17, 52). SAVED domains recognize nucleotide ligands as a monomeric unit, and divergent domains have been shown to respond to asymmetric ligands including 2′3′3′-cAAA and 3′2′-cGAMP (17, 92). Crystal structures of the CBASS receptor protein Cap4 demonstrated that the SAVED domain is a pseudodimer fusion of two ancestral CARF proteins that function in Type III CRISPR systems as sensors of cA4 and cA6 nucleotide second messengers (17). Prototypical CARF domains unite as a homodimer to sense symmetric nucleotide ligands, suggesting that duplication and fusion into the monomeric form SAVED enabled the diversification of the nucleotide ligand binding surfaces to allow for the recognition of asymmetric ligands. SAVED domains have also been identified in Type III CRISPR operons, suggesting that a conserved mechanism of nucleotide ligand recognition allows for evolutionary exchange between these two antiphage defense systems (90). In addition to STING and SAVED, some sensor domains appear to be unique to CBASS, including the Cap15 β-barrel protein that functions as one of the smallest protein units able to specifically recognize cyclic dinucleotides (51). For some CBASS receptors a single domain functions as both the sensor and effector. For example, the receptor NucC binds the ligand 3′3′3′-cAAA through a symmetric allosteric pocket created by loops at the base of the nuclease homotrimer, demonstrating how the surface of a functional domain can be co-opted for nucleotide messenger sensing and how receptor oligomers can be harnessed to sense ligands with corresponding symmetry (89).Several major families of CBASS receptors remain to be characterized at the structural level including the phospholipase CapV that responds to 3′3′-cGAMP (119) and several classes of enigmatic TM segment–containing receptors including SLATT (synthase and LOG-Smf/DprA-associating two TM) and S4TM (4 TM) proteins (51, 52). Defining the molecular basis of receptor activation in CBASS immunity will continue to provide an important foundation to understand conserved principles of nucleotide second messenger recognition in immune defense.

4.3. Nucleotide Second Messenger Sensing Controls ReceptorOligomerization and Activation

In both animal cGLR-STING and bacterial CBASS nucleotide second messenger signaling, the major mechanism of receptor activation is protein oligomerization and filament formation (Figure 4). Recent landmark studies defined the structural basis of oligomerization and activation of full-length animal STING proteins (106, 120). In cGAS-STING signaling, 2′3′-cGAMP binds deep within the central STING ligand binding pocket to induce the compact closed conformation of the homodimer. Following 2′3′-cGAMP recognition and conformational change, a transition in the connector helix between the STING ligand binding domain and the N-terminal TM helices results in a 180° rotation. These conformational changes promote head-to-head interactions between neighboring STING dimers and drive the formation of higher-order filaments along the ER membrane surface (106). In addition to 2′3′-cGAMP-induced oligomerization, trafficking of STING from the ER to Golgi via COPII (Coat Protein Complex II) vesicles is critical to initiate downstream immune signaling (1, 121–123). STING filament formation results in clustering of the unstructured STING C-terminal tails that recruit dimers of the kinase TBK1 and induce TBK1 trans-autophosphorylation and downstream immune signaling (120, 124).

The requirement of receptor oligomerization to control downstream immunity is conserved in bacterial CBASS (17). Structural analysis of bacterial Cap12 TIR-STING filament formation reveals striking conservation with the mechanism of metazoan STING activation (109). In response to the CD-NTase signal 3′3′-c-di-GMP, the bacterial STING domain adopts a compact closed conformation that exposes oligomerization interfaces and enables head-to-head STING filament formation. Bacterial TIR-STING oligomerization is further stabilized by cross-dimer contacts that occur at surfaces conserved in both bacteria and mammalian STING proteins. In CBASS immunity, TIR-STING filament formation promotes cross-dimer contacts in the TIR domain that activate the NADase catalytic site to trigger rapid NAD+ hydrolysis and inhibition of phage replication (109). Analysis of the CBASS effectors Cap4 [REase (restriction endonuclease)-SAVED] and Cap12 (TIR-SAVED) demonstrate that filament formation is also required for activation of SAVED domain-containing effectors (17, 110). Adjacent SAVED domains sandwich the bound nucleotide signals to create a stacking interaction that induces receptor filament formation and activation of appended cell death effector domains (92, 110). CBASS TM effectors including Cap15 also require oligomerization for activation and bacterial inner membrane disruption (51). Although filaments have not been observed for the receptor NucC, recognition of 3′3′3′-cAAA by this receptor controls hexamer formation that is required for effector nuclease activity (89). The large structural diversity of receptor domains that function through nucleotide second messengerinduced filament formation highlights the key role of receptor oligomerization in rapid activation of CBASS antiphage defense.

Cap4 exists in an inactive monomeric state, and recognition of the cognate CD-NTase nucleotide second messenger signal by the Cap4 SAVED domain drives oligomerization and filament formation.Cap4 oligomerization results in REase domain clustering and enzymatic activation of promiscuous dsDNA cleavage activity that degrades the host chromosome and viral DNA to small ∼17-bp fragments (17). CBASS effector Cap5, which contains the HNH-nuclease domain, functions through a similar mechanism of action where SAVEDdependent nucleotide second messenger recognition drives enzyme oligomerization and DNase effector function (17, 92). The CBASS nuclease NucC is a constitutive homotrimer with each monomer unit containing an REase active site positioned on the outer edge of the oligomeric complex. Upon binding the CD-NTase signal 3′3′3′-cAAA, NucC assembles into an active hexamer that degrades dsDNA substrates to ∼50–100-bp fragments (89). Cap4, Cap5, and NucC nucleases each rely on nucleotide second messenger–dependent oligomerization to control activation of promiscuous enzymatic domains and cleave dsDNA targets regardless of circularization, methylation pattern, or source of origin (17, 89, 92). Notably, CBASS nuclease effectors are frequently encoded in other antiphage defense systems, with the Cap4 REase domain found in Lamassu and AVAST (17, 143, 144), and NucC found in Type III CRISPR systems (89, 145, 146).

Depletion of essential metabolites is another strategy through which CBASS effectors control antiphage abortive infection. TIR domains from plants, animals, and bacteria cleave NAD to inhibit cellular redox reactions and block central metabolism (14, 147, 148). CBASS TIR effectors are fused to the nucleotide second messenger sensor domains STING (Cap12) and SAVED. Like CBASS nuclease effectors, TIR proteins exist as inactive monomers or dimers in the absence of nucleotide second messenger signaling and form active oligomerized filament complexes following nucleotide signal recognition (14, 109, 110). CBASS TIR effectors are exceptionally potent NADases in vitro,cleaving NAD+ at more than 10 times the rate of plant and animal TIR proteins involved in immune defense and causing rapid growth arrest when activated in cells (14). NAD+ cleavage is a widespread cell death mechanism in prokaryotic defense systems, with TIR domain

effectors also occurring in Pycsar, Thoeris, and SIR2 (silent information regulator 2)–based defense systems (26, 27, 149). Beyond NADases, CBASS effectors include nucleosidases that have been shown to degrade ATP (150). CBASS effectors are also predicted to include phosphatases and peptidases that may target other biomolecules required for cell viability (15, 52).

An especially diverse class of CBASS effectors is cell death proteins that disrupt the inner cell membrane (51, 119). TM domain-containing effectors (TM effectors) are some of the most common CD-NTase nucleotide second messenger receptors, making up nearly 40% of all CBASS effectors and appearing frequently in Type I (67%) and Type IV (81%) CBASS systems (15, 51). CBASS TM effectors exhibit diverse protein domain architectures including as TM segments fused to discrete nucleotide binding domains or small TM segment-only proteins with small intracellular loops. Structural and functional analysis of the CBASS effector Cap15 demonstrated that the protein contains two TM segments fused to a minimal β-barrel nucleotide second messenger binding domain (51). Cyclic dinucleotide recognition induces Cap15 oligomerization and a clustering event that causes inner membrane rupture and rapid cell death. The CBASS effector Cap14 contains TM segments fused to a SAVED domain and likely functions through similar oligomerization-dependent membrane disruption (51). Other CBASS TM effectors include SLATT4, SLATT6, and S4TM domain-containing proteins that consist of 2–4 TM segments (52). It is not known how these minimal TM effectors control nucleotide second messenger recognition or cause membrane disruption. A Caulobacter crescentus CheY-like protein involved in bacterial motility regulation recognizes 3′3′-c-di-GMP with a minimal, linear 19 amino acid motif (151),suggesting that CBASS SLATT and S4TM TM effectors may use intervening soluble protein loops to coordinate nucleotide second messenger binding. Recent analysis reveals that a TM effector in CRISPR immunity named Csx28 forms membrane pores (152), but no current evidence supports that CBASS TM effectors can form membrane-spanning pores. Instead, analysis of Cap14 and Cap15 suggests that inner membrane disruption occurs through raft-like clustering that results in large membrane lesions (51). CBASS effectors also target inner membrane integrity through enzymatic domains. CapV is a patatin-like phospholipase effector common in Type II CBASS operons that upon 3′3′-cGAMP recognition cleaves cell membrane phospholipids to control cell death and inhibit phage replication (13, 119). The targeting of cellular membrane integrity may be an especially efficient mechanism for inhibiting phage replication, as the chemical properties of inner membrane integrity are highly conserved across diverse bacteria and the precise timing of host cell lysis is critical for successful virion propagation.
6. EVOLUTION OF CBASS AND cGLR IMMUNE SYSTEMS ACROSS DOMAINS OF LIFE

Prokaryotic immune systems, including CBASS operons, tend to cluster in dynamic genomic hotspots of antiviral immunity termed defense islands (153,154) (Figure 6).While defense islands may be maintained in bacterial populations by the vertical genetic transfer of host chromosomes, they are also frequently encoded on mobile genetic elements that move through bacterial populations by diverse mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer (155, 156). In this dynamic ecosystem of genetic exchange, the evolutionary pressures of phage infection select for potent antiviral systems, drive diversification of defense island composition, and promote the spread of defense systems across divergent bacterial populations. As a result, CBASS systems are widespread in prokaryotic genomes, encoded alongside a diversity of companion defense systems, and control antiphage immunity through diverse mechanisms of nucleotide signal synthesis and Cap effector-induced cell death.

Evolution of CBASS and cGLR immune systems across domains of life. In bacteria, CBASS systems are encoded in defense islands on host chromosomes or MGEs such as prophage, transposons, and plasmids. Defense islands move through bacterial populations by vertical and horizontal gene transfer with a gene composition rapidly evolving through genetic exchange. Data in the field support two evolutionary scenarios for the acquisition of cGLR and STING genes by the metazoan lineage from ancestral CBASS systems: In scenario 1, cGLR and STING genes were acquired by a progenitor archaeon from a CBASS system in alpha-proteobacteria during endosymbiotic events that founded the eukaryotic lineage. As eukaryotes evolved, cGLRs and STING were retained by metazoans and lost in plants, fungi, and protists. In scenario 2, cGLR and STING genes were acquired by an ancestral metazoan through a rare event of horizontal gene transfer from bacteria. A further open evolutionary question is whether cGLRs and STING were acquired jointly, from a single CBASS operon, or individually, from distinct operons. cGLRs have evolved throughout animals to form a diverse family of pattern recognition receptors, and STING proteins have evolved to control different mechanisms of antiviral immunity. 6.2. Evolutionary Acquisition of cGLRs and STING by Metazoans

Structural and functional conservation establishes CBASS antiphage defense systems as the ancestral origin of animal cGLR-STING antiviral pathways (12–14). cGLR and STING genes are encoded in most animal species (11, 87, 108) and in choanoflagellates (136) but have not been identified in other eukaryotes. CD-NTase enzymes and STING nucleotide second messenger receptors by the metazoan lineage remains a major open question. Evidence in the field supports two potential evolutionary models (Figure 6):

list items.content: 1. cGLR and STING genes were members of a primordial arsenal of eukaryotic innate immune genes. This reservoir was seeded during a series of endosymbiotic events between archaea and alpha-proteobacteria that likely originated the eukaryotic lineage (157–159). As eukaryotes evolved, this repertoire of immune genes then diversified throughout different lineages, with the loss of select systems and the evolution of retained systems through domain shuffling, gene duplication, and mutation. In this model, cGLRs and STING were present in an early eukaryote and specifically lost in plant, fungi, and protist lineages.

2. cGLR and STING genes were acquired through rare cross-kingdom horizontal gene transfer events between bacteria and an early metazoan progenitor (160, 161). In support of this model, cGLR and STING genes have not been identified in plants, fungi, or the majority of unicellular eukaryotes (108). Choanoflagellates, the closest living relatives of animals, are the most divergent eukaryotes encoding STING, supporting that they may have been near the original node of acquisition of CBASS components (136).

kids.content: A further open question in the evolutionary acquisition of cGLR-STING by metazoans is whether each component gene was acquired together from a single CBASS operon or separately through individual events. In one evolutionary scenario, acquisition of a complete CD-NTase– STING operon from bacteria created a functional signaling pathway that controlled cell death as an immune response to pathogen infection. Genome evolution in the metazoan lineage could then have separated cGLR and STING genes to distinct chromosomes and enabled gene duplication and diversification events that created the current diversity of cGLR-STING signaling pathways. STING is exceptionally rare in bacteria, occurring in less than 3% of CBASS operons (14). It is therefore unclear why an evolutionary acquisition of CBASS into metazoans would include STING and not more common Cap effectors. In an alternative evolutionary scenario, STING was first acquired from bacteria and functioned alone as a receptor to sense common bacterial cyclic dinucleotide PAMPs including 3′3′-c-di-GMP and 3′3′-c-di-AMP. In support of a STING-first evolutionary event, bacterial STING receptors are the only CBASS effectors that respond to 3′3′-c-di-GMP (14), and STING-dependent sensing of foreign 3′3′-c-di-GMP and 3′3′-c-di-AMP is known to be a critical component of the animal immune response to bacterial infection (113–115). Once cells encoded a functional STING receptor to sense nucleotide second messenger signals, a strong selective advantage may have then existed to further acquire CD-NTase proteins and establish endogenous cGLR-STING signaling pathways. In either scenario, the diverse repertoire of cGLRs encoded across animals may have evolved from a signal CD-NTase progenitor or multiple distinct CD-NTases that seeded different animal cGLR lineages.

A final evolutionary puzzle is how 2′3′-cGAMP emerged as the major nucleotide second messenger in animal cGLR-STING immunity. 2′3′-cGAMP is synthesized by diverse cGLRs throughout the animal kingdom (11), but no bacterial CD-NTases have been identified that produce 2′3′-cGAMP. Although the most common CBASS signal is 3′3′-cGAMP, CD-NTases can signal through 2′–5′-linked products, suggesting that 2′3′-cGAMP may occur in bacteria as a rare signal in antiphage defense (17, 92). Early acquisition of a 2′3′-cGAMP-synthesizing CDNTase into eukaryotes may have created the foundation for the major role of this signal in animal immunity. Alternatively, 2′3′-cGAMP may have independently evolved in eukaryotes as a mechanism to discriminate endogenous signaling pathways from bacterial nucleotide second messenger detection.

Animal cGLRs are extremely diverse at the amino acid level, with most enzymes exhibiting less than 30% sequence identity. Metazoans typically encode 1–5 cGLRs; however, select phyla exhibit extreme genetic radiation, with species such as the oyster C. virginica encoding more than 200 cGLRs (11). Conversely, cGLRs have been lost in certain animal phyla, including nematodes and platyhelminthes. Intriguingly, the cGLR protein scaffold also appears to have been co-opted in animals for nonimmune functions. Widely conserved Mab21-like proteins are close structural homologs of cGLRs that lack a complete enzymatic site and appear to play a role in tissue development (162, 163). Most animals encode a single STING protein (11, 108). Unlike CBASS TIR-STING and TM-STING effectors that control cell death, animal STING proteins control downstream immunity via autophagy and the induction of antiviral gene programs. Throughout the course of metazoan evolution, STING acquired unique structural features to control animal innate immunity, including the C-terminal tail present in vertebrate STING proteins (14). The ancestral immune mechanism of STING and the protein features that control immune activation in invertebrate STING proteins remain an important area of investigation.

The use of nucleotide second messenger signals to link pathogen detection with immune activation is a conserved mechanism of antiviral immunity shared between the prokaryotic and eukaryotic kingdoms of life. Bacterial CBASS and animal cGLR-STING immune systems illustrate the unique evolutionary advantages of using nucleotide second messenger immune signals, including the co-option of fundamental nucleotidyltransferase biochemistry, the ubiquity of ribonucleotide substrates, rapid signal evolution, signal amplification, and the independent evolution of cGLR and CD-NTase proteins from downstream immune adaptor or cell death effector proteins. The discovery of the evolutionary origins of cGAS-STING signaling reveals a direct connection between animal immunity and bacterial antiphage defense and provides a framework to explain the rules that govern host-virus interactions across all domains of life.
